data.about: A 2.4 metre steel column, 400 square millimetres of solid round bar, pinned at both ends, asked to carry 54 kilonewtons. The cross-section itself is fine — it could squash at 135 kN — but a solid round bar is the worst possible shape for its area, and at this length it goes sideways long before it goes short. Two numbers put it on the sheet's chart, and the point lands far above the curve. Euler agrees and is harsher: it buckles at 4.58 kN, so the column is overloaded almost twelvefold. The view also carries the sheet's own problem honestly: the printed chart is not self-consistent, and reads about 1.6 times kinder than theory.

steps.caption: EX 10 task 4: a 2.4 metre steel column, 400 square millimetres of solid round bar, hinged at both ends, carrying 54 kN. Is it stable? The sheet wants it answered off its own buckling chart
steps.title: The exercise

steps.caption: left: the column as given — S355, 2400 mm long, A = 400 mm², N_d = 54 kN, a hinge at each end. A hinge at both ends is case a) of the strip along the top, so the buckling length is the full length
steps.title: The column

steps.caption: top left: the five cases the sheet prints beside the chart. Hinged at both ends is the plainest and the worst of the ordinary ones — the column bows into a single half wave over its whole length, so the buckling length is the length itself
steps.title: The support condition fixes l_cr

steps.caption: everything the chart needs is two numbers. Along the bottom, the buckling length divided by the square root of the area — a slenderness that does not care what shape the section is. Up the side, how hard the section is being pushed as a fraction of what it could squash at
steps.title: The two coordinates

steps.caption: right: the chart, with the lowest curve — the round solid profile, the worst shape there is for a given area, because all the material sits where it does least good. Digitised straight off the printed page, because the chart is a photograph on the sheet and not a drawing
steps.title: The sheet’s curve

steps.caption: the point (120.0, 0.399) sits high above a curve that at this slenderness is down at 0.055. The column is being asked for about 7 times what the chart allows it
steps.title: Far above the curve — it buckles

steps.caption: the theory curve overlaid, for the same shape. It is the whole of buckling in one line: the load a pinned strut can take falls with the SQUARE of its length, and depends on the stiffness E and the shape I — never on the strength of the steel. The two curves do not coincide, and that is a fault in the sheet, not in the theory
steps.title: Euler agrees, and is harsher

steps.caption: nothing about the steel helps — a higher grade buckles at exactly the same load, because only E and I appear. What helps is shortening the buckling length or moving the material away from the axis. Both are drawn: three restraints turn one 2.4 m column into four 0.6 m ones, and the same 400 mm² rolled into a thin tube is three and a half times better shaped
steps.title: b) How to stop it buckling

steps.caption: It fails. l_cr/√A = 120.0 and N_d/(A·f_cd) = 0.3993 put the point far above the round-solid curve, and Euler gives N_cr = 4.58 kN against 54 kN demanded — a factor of 11.79. It would have to be about 0.70 m long instead of 2.4
steps.title: The answer

data.title: EX 10.4 — the column buckles, and by a factor of twelve
